about.title: Fullerton Car Accident Claims
about.longDescription: Fullerton sits at a busy crossroads of north Orange County, and its streets show it. In 2025, the city recorded 734 injury collisions, with 1,135 people hurt and 4 lives lost. Public collision records point to Harbor Boulevard, Euclid Street, southbound SR-57, and Orangethorpe Avenue as the corridors where the most crashes are reported, and the numbers tend to climb on Friday evenings between 5 and 7 p.m. as commuters head home. If one of those crashes was yours, you are likely juggling doctor visits, a damaged car, and calls from an adjuster you did not ask to hear from. LawProactive exists to take one item off that list. We are not a law firm. We connect you, at no cost, with an independent California personal injury attorney who handles Fullerton car accident claims on contingency. That attorney can review your police report, help preserve evidence before it disappears, and deal with the other driver's insurer so you do not have to.

whyChoose.title: Why Fullerton Drivers Reach Out to LawProactive

items.title: Two-Year Clock, Sometimes Much Shorter
items.desc: California gives most car accident victims two years to file, but a claim involving a city, county, or Caltrans vehicle or roadway can require notice in as little as six months. Getting connected early keeps those deadlines from becoming a problem.

items.title: Partial Fault Doesn't Close the Door
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, you can still recover even if you were partly to blame; your share of fault simply reduces the amount. An attorney can push back when an insurer tries to inflate your percentage.

items.title: No Cap on Pain and Suffering, No Upfront Fee
items.desc: California places no limit on non-economic damages in ordinary car accident cases, and the attorneys in our network work on contingency. You pay nothing unless there is a recovery.

items.question: I was rear-ended on the 57 near Orangethorpe. Does it matter that it happened on a freeway?
items.answer: For a crash between private drivers, the location mainly matters for evidence, such as CHP reports and nearby camera footage. If a government vehicle was involved or a roadway condition contributed, however, a separate claim against that public entity may need to be filed within six months. An attorney can sort out quickly whether that shorter deadline applies to you.

items.question: The other driver's insurance company keeps calling for a recorded statement. Should I give one?
items.answer: You are not required to give the other insurer a recorded statement, and it is generally wise to decline until you have spoken with an attorney. Adjusters are trained to ask questions in ways that can later be used to reduce your claim. Focus instead on keeping photos, medical records, repair estimates, and witness contact information in one place.

items.question: The police report says I was partly at fault. Is my claim over?
items.answer: Not in California. The state follows pure comparative fault, meaning you can still recover damages even if you share some of the blame, with your award reduced by your percentage of responsibility. Police reports are also not the final word; an attorney can gather additional evidence that tells a fuller story of what happened.
